verses.text: For when gods and mortal humans were settling their dispute
at Mecone, Prometheus eagerly divided a great ox
and set the portions before them, trying to deceive Zeus.
In one portion he placed the meat and the organs rich with fat
inside the hide, covering them with the ox’s stomach;
in the other, he arranged the ox’s white bones with cunning skill
and laid them out, covered with shining fat.
Then the father of gods and humans said to him:
“Son of Iapetus, most glorious of all lords,
my friend, how unevenly you have divided the portions!”
So Zeus mocked him, Zeus whose plans never fail.
Prometheus, with his twisting schemes, answered him
with a gentle smile, still mindful of his cunning trick:
“Zeus, greatest and most glorious of the everlasting gods,
choose whichever portion your heart urges you to take.”
So he spoke deceitfully. But Zeus, whose plans never fail,
recognized the trick and saw it clearly; in his heart he foresaw troubles
for mortal humans, troubles that would indeed come true.
With both hands Zeus lifted the white fat.
Rage filled his mind, and anger reached his heart
when he saw the ox’s white bones laid out in that cunning trick.
Ever since then, the peoples of the earth have offered the immortal gods
white bones burned on altars fragrant with sacrifice.
Deeply angered, Zeus the cloud-gatherer said to Prometheus:
“Son of Iapetus, clever beyond all others,
my friend, you still have not forgotten your cunning tricks!”
So spoke Zeus in anger, Zeus whose plans never fail.
From then on, always remembering the trick,
he withheld the power of tireless fire in ash wood
from mortal humans who live upon the earth.
But the noble son of Iapetus, Prometheus, deceived him
by stealing the far-shining glow of tireless fire
in a hollow fennel stalk. The theft bit deep into the heart
of Zeus, who thunders on high, and filled his heart with anger
when he saw fire’s far-shining glow among humans.
At once, in return for fire, Zeus made an evil for humans.
For famous Hephaestus, lame in both legs, shaped earth
into the likeness of a modest young woman, following the plan of Zeus, son of Cronus.
The bright-eyed goddess Athena dressed and belted her
in a silvery robe, and over her head she lowered a veil
with her own hands, intricately worked, a wonder to see.
Around her head, garlands of flowers from the fresh-grown grass
were placed by Pallas Athena, lovely garlands.
Athena also placed a golden crown upon her head,
which famous Hephaestus, lame in both legs, had made himself,
working skillfully with his hands to please his father Zeus.
On it were crafted many intricate figures, a wonder to see:
creatures of the many kinds the land and sea sustain.
He set many of these upon it, and great beauty shone from them,
marvelous figures, like living creatures with voices of their own.
When Hephaestus had made this beautiful evil in exchange for the good,
he led her out to where the other gods and humans were,
glorying in the finery given by bright-eyed Athena, daughter of a mighty father.
Wonder seized the immortal gods and mortal humans
when they saw this deadly trap, which humans had no means to escape.

uncertainties: Verse 563 is disputed: Μελίῃσι may refer to ash trees or ash wood, or to the Melian nymphs. The translation follows the ash-wood interpretation.
Verses 576–577 are marked for deletion in the supplied Greek; they are translated here because every assigned verse was requested.
